question: Tell me about a time when you invested in an employee's development. What did you invest in and why? What was the outcome? Can you share an example where investing in an employee's development didn't work out?

raiseTranscript.text: When a new teammate joined our project, I spent extra time pairing with them on their first two features and walked through our codebase patterns.
About six hours a week for a month plus written notes on common pitfalls. They shipped their first ticket two weeks earlier than the team expected.
And the case that didn't work?
I tried the same approach with another new hire who already knew the stack; they got frustrated and asked for less help. I stopped after two sessions.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you invested in someone's development
Paired with new teammate on first features, 6 hrs/wk for a month, created notes on pitfalls
Outcome: new hire shipped first ticket two weeks early
Quote: 'They asked for less help after two sessions'
Follow-up: Why did you stop? 'They already knew the patterns so I switched to async reviews'
junior.raiseFeedback: Candidate described a concrete, time-bounded investment in a peer rather than a direct report, which is appropriate at this level. The positive case shows they tracked output (first ticket shipped early) and adjusted when the recipient signaled they needed less help. The negative example demonstrates they recognized over-investment and stopped without forcing the approach. Biggest strength is the willingness to course-correct quickly instead of persisting with a mismatched plan.

lowerTranscript.text: I once helped a classmate with their homework by explaining the assignment.
What was the outcome for them?
They got a better grade. I don't really have an example where it didn't work.

lowerNotes: Follow-up: Asked for work example, candidate stayed with school story
junior.lowerFeedback: Story stays in academic territory and never connects to workplace impact or measurable change in the other person's output. Candidate could not produce an example where development effort failed, which removes any signal on learning or adjustment. The investment described (one-time homework help) is too light to show sustained ownership. Main gap is absence of any follow-through or outcome tracking beyond a single grade.

raiseTranscript.text: A mid-level engineer on another team wanted to move into distributed systems work. I created a six-week reading list and reviewed their design docs weekly.

They led the next service migration and the team cited their design as the template. The negative case was a different engineer who wanted the same path but never completed the first reading; after three check-ins with no progress I closed the loop and suggested they focus on current role priorities.

raiseNotes: Q: Invested in employee's development
Built 6-week reading list + weekly design reviews for cross-team engineer
Outcome: engineer led service migration; design became team template
Negative: different engineer never completed readings, effort stopped after three check-ins
Quote: 'Suggested they focus on current role priorities'
senior.raiseFeedback: Candidate chose a cross-team target and tied the investment to a specific business outcome (service migration). They tracked completion and adjusted when the second person showed no progress, demonstrating boundary-setting. The negative case shows they did not continue investing time once signals were clear. Primary strength is linking personal development to a concrete deliverable the broader team later adopted.

lowerTranscript.text: I gave a teammate some articles on system design because they asked.
Did anything change in their work?
They said it was helpful. I don't have a case where it didn't land.

lowerNotes: Follow-up: Any measurable change? Candidate could not name one
senior.lowerFeedback: Investment is passive (shared links) with no structured plan or follow-up. Candidate cannot point to any observable change in the other person's scope or output. Lack of a failed example removes evidence of judgment on when to stop. Main gap is absence of ownership over the result beyond the initial gesture.

raiseTranscript.text: One of my directs wanted to move from IC to tech lead. I put them on a project with two junior engineers, gave them explicit coaching on delegation, and reviewed their 1:1 notes weekly for three months.

They were promoted and the two juniors both improved their velocity by 30 percent. The case that didn't work was an engineer who wanted the same track but resisted delegating; after two cycles of feedback with no change I moved them to a pure IC track and documented the decision.

raiseNotes: Q: Invested in direct's development
Assigned project with two reports, weekly coaching on delegation, reviewed 1:1 notes for 3 months
Outcome: promoted; two juniors velocity +30%
Negative: resisted delegation, moved to IC track after two feedback cycles
Follow-up: How did you decide to stop? 'Documented decision and aligned with their skip'
manager.raiseFeedback: Candidate used a real project assignment and measurable coaching cadence to develop a direct report. Positive outcome includes both the individual's promotion and downstream team impact. The negative case shows timely recognition of resistance and a clear pivot to a better-fit role. Core strength is treating development as a managed program with exit criteria rather than open-ended mentoring.

lowerTranscript.text: I encouraged one of my reports to take a course and approved the budget.
They completed it. I haven't had a situation where development didn't pay off.

lowerNotes: Follow-up: Any change in responsibilities? Candidate had none
manager.lowerFeedback: Investment is limited to budget approval with no ongoing coaching or outcome tracking. Candidate cannot describe any shift in the person's responsibilities or results. Absence of a failed case suggests either no real development attempts or unwillingness to discuss them. Primary gap is treating development as a transaction instead of an accountable process.

raiseTranscript.text: We had a leadership gap in our platform org. I created a six-month rotation program for three high-potential directors, assigned each a P&L owner as sponsor, and tied their promotion case to org-wide metrics.

Two were promoted into director roles; platform reliability improved 25 percent under their ownership. The third did not show the required strategic thinking after four months; we moved them back to their original org and replaced them with another candidate.

raiseNotes: Q: Invested in employee development at scale
Built 6-month rotation with P&L sponsors for 3 directors, tied to org metrics
Outcome: 2 promoted, platform reliability +25%
Negative: one lacked strategic thinking, moved back after 4 months
Follow-up: How did you choose the replacement? 'Used the same criteria and pulled from a bench we had pre-identified'
exec.raiseFeedback: Candidate designed a structured, multi-person program tied to business metrics rather than one-off coaching. Positive results include both individual promotions and measurable platform improvement. The negative case shows they made a data-driven call to remove someone from the track without prolonged investment. Key strength is creating repeatable leverage through a program instead of relying on personal heroics.

lowerTranscript.text: I told my VPs to spend more time mentoring their directs.
A couple of people got promoted over the next year. I don't recall a case where it failed.

lowerNotes: Outcome: 'A couple of people got promoted'
Follow-up: Any org-level metric or program? Candidate had none
exec.lowerFeedback: Action is a directive to others with no personal structure, tracking, or accountability. Outcome is vague and cannot be linked to the candidate's investment. Lack of a failed example removes evidence of strategic judgment on talent. Main gap is absence of any scalable mechanism or measured business impact.

diagnostic.junior: Peer or intern level, time-bounded help
diagnostic.manager: Direct report with role change and team impact
diagnostic.exec: Multi-person program tied to org metrics

diagnostic.senior: Closed loop after no progress on readings
diagnostic.manager: Moved to IC track after two cycles
diagnostic.exec: Removed from rotation after four months with replacement ready
After four months with documented decision
